paragraphs.text: [Meizhan](yancha:meizhan) is a Fujian cultivar that came from Anxi. This leaf grew in the Wuyi Mountains and was made as [Wuyi rock tea](yancha:definition), a name only tea from that area may carry. Meizhan is less well known than Rougui and Shui Xian, and it is not one of the four famous bushes of Wuyi. Like other rock tea, it was twisted into long strips and finished over charcoal. The [roast](yancha:making) is given in several rounds with weeks or months of rest between them, which dries the leaf so it keeps.

This tea was made in 2024, so it is two years old. Rock tea is labelled by its [roast level](yancha:roast-levels), and the heavier the roast, the longer a tea is said to stay good. Stored tea is kept sealed, dry and cool, because damp is what makes it [go green again](yancha:ageing).

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: Roast and stone fruit, a mineral, rocky texture and a long, sweet, mouth-watering finish. Light roast is bright and floral, medium roast fruity and rounded, full roast charcoal, wood and roasted nuts. Da Hong Pao is often floral, Rougui spicy with cinnamon, young Shui Xian sweet and smooth, and old-bush Shui Xian woody and mossy.
